html:
A Buddhist temple in Nara, once one of the Seven Great Temples of the old southern capital and the clan temple of the Fujiwara. It began in 669 at Yamashina, near today's Kyoto, founded by Kagami-no-Ōkimi, wife of Fujiwara no Kamatari, to pray for her husband's recovery from illness. In 672 it moved to Fujiwara-kyō, the first Japanese capital laid out on the grid of Chang'an, and in 710 to its present site on the east side of the new capital, Heijō-kyō, now Nara. Kamatari's son Fujiwara no Fuhito named it "the temple that generates blessings", after the Vimalakirti Sutra. It is the head temple of the Hossō school, the Japanese form of Yogācāra Buddhism.

The temple rose with the family. Fuhito's daughter married Emperor Shōmu and became Empress Kōmyō; she ordered the first five-storey pagoda in 730 and the Western Golden Hall in 734, and a later chronicle says she founded Japan's first dispensary and welfare house here. When the capital moved to Heian-kyō in 794, temples such as Tōdai-ji declined, but Kōfuku-ji kept its weight through its Fujiwara patrons and pressed the imperial government, at times by force. It controlled other temples too, among them Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto. Taira forces burned it with Tōdai-ji in 1180, during the Genpei War, and war and fire destroyed it many more times.

What stands today is mostly from its medieval rebuildings: the three-storey pagoda of 1185, the North Octagonal Hall of 1210, the East Golden Hall of 1425 and the five-storey pagoda of 1426. Some buildings, among them one of the three golden halls and the great south gate, were never rebuilt; the Central Golden Hall was rebuilt in 2018. Its treasures include a dry-lacquer statue of Asura, one of the Eight Legions of guardian deities, and statues of the Buddha's ten great disciples. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
